(01:09:40): And we have this new feature, Healthspan, that we just launched with our new hardware. And basically, what it's trying to do is help you have this reward loop, between your behaviors and activities that you're doing today, and what means for how healthy you're going to be in 20, 30, 40 years. (01:09:59): And so, we have something similar where we have this, we call it the Amoeba. It has your WHOOP age in it. It has colors, and moves around, and that changes, based on how your behaviors and your activities change, every single day. (01:10:12): And the colors change when you're doing better, and when you're doing worse. And you can kind of see it all broken down, how you sleep, your VO2 Max, the consistency of your sleep, how much time you're spending in different heart rate zones, how much time you're spending in strength training, things like that. (01:10:27): And we found that, again, it's just this incredibly powerful reward loop, because we're taking something that historically has been really, really hard, which is, "When I make healthy changes today, not only do I not see the results of those for decades, but the short term reward loop of those often feels pretty bad, because change is hard, and it feels bad before it feels good." (01:10:46): And trying to build that reward loop that is more rewarding for people to see those numbers change, and to see those colors change, so that they're actually able to make those changes, and see that progress, and feel really good about it.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得 WHOOP 有一样东西做得特别好。我认为 WHOOP 上最有趣的一种"反奖励循环"是关于酒精的。WHOOP 有一套恢复系统。你每天早上会得到一个恢复分数。它是红、黄、绿三色，基本上代表你恢复得怎么样，以及你准备好迎接这一天了吗。(01:08:05)：如果你喝酒，而且戴着 WHOOP，你很快就会知道，只要你一喝酒，就会得到红色恢复。这很有意思，因为喝酒的人以前也不是没有宿醉，或者他们知道喝酒会扰乱睡眠。这些对人们来说都不是新闻，但看到那个红色分数时，就是有种感觉，就是让人感觉很糟。它对人有种非常深刻的情感冲击。(01:08:38)：而当你看到绿色分数时，感觉就很棒。就像是"噢，我做对了什么事，我在照顾好自己。我是个健康的人。"我和会员们聊天时一直听到这种说法，也听到人们说"我喝酒的问题已经很多年了。直到我用了 WHOOP，才真正控制住了我的饮酒。"(01:08:58)：我对此再次感到惊讶，因为我就想"你之前已经拥有了所有你需要的信息"，但就是早上醒来看到那个红色分数这件事，它居然能够盖过最初驱使人们去喝酒的那些动因。(01:09:14)：然后，我觉得，持续拥有这些数据也很重要，你可以回看自己的数据，看到"哦，那天是红色的一天，那天就是我做了那件事的日子。"而这其实是我们一直在尝试用更长期的方式去做的事情。(01:09:28)：因为当你拥有这些短的奖励循环时，会更容易，就像"我做了一件事。"然后我立刻要么得到奖励（绿色恢复），要么得到反奖励（红色恢复），而这正在改变我的行为。(01:09:40)：另……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you're using all these habit building tactics that folks have been using historically, to get you to check your Instagram likes, and your Facebook posts for actual good, for helping people live longer and happier. That makes me very happy. (01:11:14): Is there an example of doing this sort of thing with your team, of helping them build, and you talk about AI learning to use Claude, ChatGPT?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢你把历史上那些用来让人去刷 Instagram 点赞、刷 Facebook 动态的那些习惯养成策略，用在真正好的地方，帮助人们活得更久、更快乐。这让我很开心。(01:11:14)：有没有一个在团队里做这种事、帮助大家养成的例子，就是你之前聊到的让团队学习使用 Claude、ChatGPT 的 AI？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, I think with AI, I think a lot of it's just shouting people out, right? When somebody is using AI to solve a problem that they wouldn't have used AI before, give them a shout-out in the team meeting, let them demo that. (01:11:37): Again, make them feel like a million bucks for doing the thing. And people respond to that, people will see, I mean, maybe it's because I work at WHOOP, and we're all obsessed with reward loops, so we're all choosing them.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得在 AI 方面，很多其实就是公开表扬，对吧？当有人用 AI 解决了一个以前不会用 AI 解决的问题时，在团队会议上表扬他们，让他们做个演示。(01:11:37)：再次，让他们因为做了这件事而感觉棒极了。人们会有反应的，大家会看到——我是说，也许是因为我在 WHOOP 工作，我们都对奖励循环着迷，所以我们都在用这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or reward looping each other. "Here's your reward."
turns.zh: 或者彼此之间做奖励循环。"这是给你的奖励。"

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: No, exactly. But no, people see that, and people respond to it. I think another example is something that I think about a lot, and is relevant to our conversation about, just how you build teams that can do hard things, is how you encourage people to take care of themselves outside of work. And it's something that I'm always trying to model for my team, and make it really visible the ways that I'm doing this, and sort of having my hobbies, and my other various things. (01:12:18): And as a result, I also try to reward, have these reward loops, when I see people on my team doing the same thing. Because I think people, bosses often inadvertently create reward loops for, "Oh, this person, they had to stay up till two o'clock to get it done, but they got it done." When you create those reward loops, that's the behavior that people start mimicking. (01:12:38): And so, I try to do the opposite. I try to find ways that I really am impressed with my team, and the ways that they take care of themselves outside of work, because I think that makes them better at their jobs, frankly, and just happier humans. So there's a PM on my team, Emily, who teaches at Handlebar. She's a fitness instructor in her spare time. (01:12:59): And so, whenever we have a long meeting, I'll be like, "Oh, Emily, why don't you lead stretches, to get the energy level in the room up? Just nothing serious, just for a minute, before we start the meeting." And it's kind of fun. Everyone has a laugh about it, "Emily's doing her thing," and I'll be like, "Everyone, come check out Emily at Handlebar in Charlestown this Saturday, 10 a.m." (01:13:22): And by the way, you all out there in the podcast world should do that if you're in the Boston area, she's great. Shout-out to Emily. But it's things like that. It's just finding these small ways to, because people are already laughing, people are already smiling, we're doing this silly thing, everyone's in a good mood, and I'm like, "Boom, perfect time to give someone a shout-out, and make them feel like a million bucks for doing something, that in many cases, they might think, 'Oh, am I allowed to have this other job outside work? Is this okay?'" And so yeah, you got to proactively build those reward loops.
turns.zh: 不，没错。但我说，人们看到这个，就会有反应。我觉得另一个例子是我经常思考、也和我们关于"如何建立能做困难事情的团队"的对话相关的，就是你如何鼓励人们在下班后照顾好自己。这是我一直在努力为团队做榜样的事，让我做这些的方式变得真正可见，包括我的爱好，以及其他各种事情。(01:12:18)：因此，当我看到团队里有人做同样的事时，我也会试着奖励、建立这些奖励循环。因为我觉得，人们、老板们常常无意中建立了这样的奖励循环——"哦，这个人，他们熬到凌晨两点才把它做完，但他们做完了。"当你建立那种奖励循环时，那就会成为人们开始模仿的行为。(01:12:38)：所以，我试着反其道而行。我试着找到真正让我佩服我的团队的方式，以及他们下班后照顾好自己的方式，因为坦白说，我觉得那能让他们把工作做得更好，也让人更快乐。我团队里有个产品经理叫 Emily，她在 Handlebar 教课。她业余时间是个健身教练。(01:12:59)：所以，每当我们开长会时，我就会说"哦，Emily，要不你带大家做做拉伸，把房间里的能量提起来？就轻松一点，开会前做一分钟就好。"这还挺有趣的。大家都会笑，说"Emily 在干她的活儿"，然后我就会说"各位，这周六上午 10 点来 Charlestown 的 Handlebar 看 Emily 的课。"(01:13:22)：顺便说一句，播客世界里的各位如果身在波士顿地区，也应该去，她很棒。给 Emily 点个赞。但就是诸如此类的事。就是找到这些小方法，因为人们已经在笑了、已经在微笑了，我们在做这件傻乎乎的事，大家都心情很好，而我就会想"砰，完……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the reward loop of Emily getting this shout-out right now. This is so meta.
turns.zh: 我喜欢 Emily 现在得到这个表扬的奖励循环。这太元（meta）了。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Ultimate reward.
turns.zh: 终极奖励。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have a full class coming up in Boston. Is there anything else along those lines? Because that was really interesting? And also, people, I know managers already kind of do this, just promoting. (01:14:06): But so, I think the core lesson here is, focus on things you want to encourage more. Less so, "Hey, they worked the weekend, they got it done, so awesome. Thank you for doing that." (01:14:16): You're saying that's almost an anti-pattern, because you don't necessarily want that as a habit. So it's more like, shift your reward announcements to things you actually, intentionally want to create, in a new team.
turns.zh: 你在波士顿有一整节课要开了。还有什么类似的事情吗？因为那真的很有趣？而且，我也知道，经理们其实已经在做这种事了，就是表扬。(01:14:06)：但我觉得这里的核心经验是，把注意力放在你更想鼓励的事情上。少一点像"嘿，他们周末加班，把事情做完了，太棒了。谢谢你做了这件事。"(01:14:16)：你是说这几乎是个反模式，因为你不一定想把那当成一种习惯。所以更像是，把你的奖励宣布转向你真正、有意想要在一个新团队里创造的东西。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, and just be really, really thoughtful about it.
turns.zh: 是的，而且要对这件事非常、非常用心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, okay. So let's come back to the taking care of yourself, because that's something else that came up, almost everyone mentioned this. So you're doing a good job with this, of finding time to take care of yourself, and modeling that for other people. (01:14:39): Specifically, a lot of people commented on how you create space for creativity. And I think, to a lot of people, a lot of PMs, especially, is just, "I have no time for anything. I just have meetings, back to back, all day. I barely have time to go to the bathroom or eat." (01:14:53): And I'm curious to hear just how you do this. How do you create space in your day for creative work, and deep work, and thinking outside of the meeting?
turns.zh: 好，好。那我们回到"照顾好自己"这个话题，因为这是另一个被提到的事，几乎每个人都提到了。你在这方面做得很好，找到时间照顾自己，并为他人树立榜样。(01:14:39)：具体来说，很多人评论了你如何为创造力创造空间。我觉得对很多人，尤其是很多产品经理来说，就是"我根本没时间做任何事。我整天就是会议连着会议。我连上厕所或吃饭的时间都几乎没有。"(01:14:53)：我很好奇你是怎么做到的。你如何在一天中为创造性工作、深度工作和会议之外的思考腾出空间？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny. I'm glad to hear people think I'm good at this, because I'm terrible at organizing events. My team's always, "Oh, we should do a fun event." I'm like, "Yeah, that's a great idea." (01:15:10): And then I don't organize it. So I like to think, I do this in other ways. And I do think one of them is just in modeling, how to carve out space for things, and a couple of things. I think there's the creativity, which for me is probably more outside of work. For me, it's creativity. (01:15:29): But again, it's a big part of me as a manager, what I think I can help people with is, back to the point of behavioral activation, understanding what the things are that a person needs to be happy, to be their best self, to be a high functioning person. That depends on their values, it depends on a lot of things about them. So for Emily, it's fitness, it's teaching, it's these things. For me, it's having my crafts that I do, my illustration, my writing, my reading, all of these sorts of things. (01:15:59): I think that that's the first step is just, as a leader, understanding what those are for people on your team. And then, as I said, modeling it. (01:16:09): I try to always tell people, "Here's how I'm doing these things." I talk about them, so it's really normalized, because I think a lot of PMs are like, "Oh my gosh, I'm so busy. I have no time. I'm in meetings all day." But that's a little bit self-inflicted, I think. (01:16:24): At some point, you have to be the one responsible for getting yourself out of the weeds, and it's hard to do, but it is doable. So I think, just showing people that it's possible, showing people that you can do these things. And I talk about them, I bring them to lessons. (01:16:43): I have a book club that I sometimes require at work, and then I say, "Maybe I don't need to require this anymore," but ways to just make it really visible, make sure people know that I'm doing it, and then ask them about it. (01:16:56): If I, in my one on one lens, and I'm checking in with people, I'm asking them, "What do you do for joy? Are you doing something every single day that's bringing you joy in your life?" And if they say no, I'm like, "That's a problem. What are we going to do about that? And do you even know what those things are?" (01:17:13): Because I think a lot of people don't, and a lot of people, it's great. They're like, "Oh, I need to be getting X number of hours of exercise, X hours of sleep. I know I need to eat lunch right at 12:00, or else I turn into a pumpkin." (01:17:26): If it's somebody who knows what all those things are, and you're just there to kind of help them carve out time, that's one thing. But I think, and a lot of times, people don't even know. Then you kind of behavioral activation them, where you're like, "All right, well, why don't you try some things, and get back to me, and let me know what seemed to work, what seemed to make a difference?" (01:17:43): But I do think so much of it is like a permission structure, because people feel the pressure to be like, "Oh, I'm so busy, I'm so busy, I'm in meetings all day. (01:17:50): I can't decline these meetings. I can't not do these things." So in many ways, I think just modeling, it gives them the permission structure to start to take back their life.
turns.zh: 是啊，这挺有意思的。我很高兴听人们觉得我擅长这个，因为我在组织活动方面糟透了。我的团队总是说"哦，我们应该搞个有趣的活动。"我就说"对，这主意太棒了。"(01:15:10)：然后我就不去组织了。所以我想，我是通过其他方式来做这件事的。我觉得其中之一就是以身作则，展示如何为事情腾出空间，有那么几个方面。我觉得创造力这一块，对我而言可能更多是在工作之外。对我来说，就是创造力。(01:15:29)：但再说一次，作为管理者，我能帮助人们的重要部分之一，回到"行为激活"那个点上，就是理解一个人要快乐、要成为最好的自己、要高效运转，所需要的东西是什么。这取决于他们的价值观，取决于他们身上很多东西。所以对 Emily 来说，是健身、是教学、是这些事。对我来说，是做我的手艺——我的插画、我的写作、我的阅读，所有这类事情。(01:15:59)：我觉得第一步就是，作为领导者，去理解团队里每个人的这些需求是什么。然后，如我所说，以身作则。(01:16:09)：我尽量总是告诉人们"我是怎么做这些事的。"我会聊这些，所以它真的就被常态化了，因为我觉得很多产品经理就像"噢天哪，我太忙了。我一点时间都没有。我整天都在开会。"但我觉得那有点是自找的。(01:16:24)：在某个时刻，你必须自己负责把自己从琐事中拉出来，这很难做到，但确实是可以做到的。所以我觉得，就是向人们展示这是可能的，向人们展示你可以做这些事。我会聊这些，我会把它们带到课程里。(01:16:43)：我有一个读书会，我有时会在工作中要求参加，然后我又说"也许我不需要再强制要求了"，但总之就是用各种方式让它真正可见，确保人们知道我在做，然后问他们做得怎么样。(01:16:56)：我……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see why people love working for you. Being asked in your one on one, "Have you done anything today that brings you joy? And if you haven't, that's a problem." Wow.
turns.zh: 我能理解为什么人们喜欢为你工作。在一对一谈话中被问到"你今天做了什么能给你带来快乐的事吗？如果没做，那就是个问题。"哇。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: It's important. It's what life's all out. Why are we here, if it's just to toil, and be miserable?
turns.zh: 这很重要。这就是人生的全部意义。如果我们来这儿只是为了苦干、受罪，那我们为什么还要在这儿？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also, they will be better people at work, and they'll do better work. I think that's, tell me, correct me if I'm wrong, but it feels like that's an element of this.
turns.zh: 而且，他们在工作中会成为更好的人，也会把工作做得更好。我觉得，告诉我，如果我说错了请纠正我，但这感觉像是其中的一个要素。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Well, and it is so funny, because so much of this stuff, it's obvious when you apply it to an athletic context. And obviously, I talked about the recovery score. This concept of athletes need to recover is very obvious. No one, I think, would argue with that. (01:18:39): If you're just pushing yourself at 100% of your physical capacity all the time, not only are you going to burn out, but you're literally going to suffer performance decline. And in the same way, I think in the athletic world, there's so much more, just acceptance of, I don't even want to say limits, but just like, you have to take the time to do the things you need to be your best. And that's not just running into the wall all day. (01:19:11): And I think we forget that at work, but I think the analog is 100% there. I also think about this with, in terms of being able to have creative breakthroughs of any kind, it's just so important to have active rest. It's so important to have heads downtime. This stuff is all very well documented. We know it all, but we just come up with excuses to not give it to ourselves. I think it's kind of self-sabotage, at a certain point.
turns.zh: 嗯，这很有意思，因为很多这类东西，一旦套用到运动场景里就显而易见了。显然，我提到了恢复分数。运动员需要恢复这个概念非常明显。我觉得没人会反对这一点。(01:18:39)：如果你一直以 100% 的体能去逼迫自己，你不仅会透支（burnout），而且字面意义上会出现表现下滑。同样地，我觉得在运动世界里，人们更能接受——我甚至不想说"极限"，而是说，你必须花时间去做那些让你达到最佳状态所需要做的事。那不是整天往墙上撞。(01:19:11)：而我觉得我们在工作中忘了这一点，但我认为类比是完全成立的。我还会从另一个角度想这个问题，就是无论哪种创造性突破，拥有"主动休息"都极其重要。拥有放空的时间极其重要。这些都有充分的文献记载。我们都知道，但我们就是给自己找借口不去给自己这些时间。我觉得在某种程度上，这有点像是自我破坏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely come up with excuses not to do that, and work all the time. So I could use this advice myself.
turns.zh: 我绝对会给自己找借口不去做那件事，然后一直工作。所以我自己也需要这条建议。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: And that's why, here's the thing, here's the thing. The Reason I'm so regimented about this is because, if I'm not, I will fall apart. There's this quote, I can't remember where I saw this, but I love it. It's like, "I have exercised the demons from my head, but they are outside and they are doing pushups." (01:19:59): The threat of the demons coming back is always there. And so, I take this stuff really seriously, because I know, if I let myself start to slide into, I'm not doing the things I need to do to take care of myself, I'm going to have a bad time. The walls are going to start closing in around me. (01:20:18): And I'm not shy about that. To me, there's no point in torturing myself, and just working so hard, and having no room for joy, and having no room for creativity. Even just from a practical standpoint, I'm just not going to succeed.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么，听我说，听我说。我之所以对这件事如此自律，是因为如果我不这样，我就会崩溃。有一句名言，我记不得在哪看到的了，但我很喜欢。大意是"我已经把心里的恶魔赶了出去，但它们在外面，正在做俯卧撑。"(01:19:59)：恶魔卷土重来的威胁始终存在。所以我非常认真地对待这件事，因为我知道，如果我放任自己开始滑向——不再做那些照顾自己需要做的事——我就会过得糟糕。墙壁会开始向我逼近。(01:20:18)：我对这一点毫不避讳。对我来说，折磨自己、拼命工作、不给快乐留空间、不给创造力留空间，毫无意义。即便单从实际角度看，我也根本不会成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This comes back to your point about, I think it was called behavioral activation, doing the thing. Instead of waiting for you to feel a certain feeling, do the thing that will make you feel that way.
turns.zh: 这又回到了你那个关于"行为激活"的观点，就是去做那件事。与其等着自己产生某种感觉，不如去做那件能让你产生那种感觉的事。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. As maybe a final area, but I have a few more questions after this, so maybe not. The final area is AI. I am happy that we waited this long to get deep into AI. We're not going to spend a lot of time here. You wrote a whole guest post about this. You did How I AI to talk through some of this stuff. (01:21:03): But when we were talking earlier, you said that you think people still are completely undervaluing the power AI could have on their ability to learn, and improve themselves. And I know you spent a lot of time on this, with all these GPTs you've built. (01:21:17): Just talk about the sense of how much you think people still under-appreciate how much power there is in AI, and helping them become better.
turns.zh: 好。这可能是最后一个话题了，但之后我还有几个问题，所以也许不是。最后一个话题是 AI。我很高兴我们等了这么久才深入聊 AI。我们不会在这里花太多时间。你为此写了一整篇客座文章。你做了 How I AI 来梳理其中一些内容。(01:21:03)：但我们之前聊的时候，你说你认为人们仍然完全低估了 AI 对他们学习能力和自我提升能力所能产生的影响。我知道你花了很多时间在这上面，建了所有这些 GPT。(01:21:17)：就谈谈你的感受吧——你觉得人们仍然在多大程度上低估了 AI 中蕴含的力量，以及它帮助人们变得更好的能力。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah. I think we are not being nearly creative enough, when it comes to how to think about learning with AI. And I think, you hear people worry about entry level jobs, and when you think about an entry level job, it is sort of inefficient by design, because you have taken analyst, sort of a classic entry level role. (01:21:49): They're doing grunt work, they're doing really tedious work, but they're getting a lot of reps in, because that's exactly how you learn the judgment to do higher level jobs well. And I hear this in creative fields too. I hear this from every, I certainly feel this way. (01:22:05): The work that I did in the beginning of my career, it didn't feel like it was all that important, in terms of the impact it was having, but it did feel like it was transformative, in terms of my own judgment and my own taste, and how I think about just making very quick judgment calls. (01:22:27): Now, I just wouldn't have been able to do that, if I didn't spend years learning. I used to do social media, the skill of having to condense something that I want to say into 120 characters, or whatever it used to be on old Twitter, 240, I can't remember.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得在"如何用 AI 来学习"这件事上，我们的创造力还远远不够。我觉得你听人们担心初级岗位，而当你想到一个初级岗位时，它在设计上本身就是低效的，因为你拿分析师——一个经典的初级角色——来说。(01:21:49)：他们在做苦力活，做非常枯燥的工作，但他们获得了大量的重复练习（reps），因为那正是你学会做好更高阶工作所需的判断力的方式。我在创意领域也听到这种说法。我从每个人那里都听到，我自己当然也有这种感觉。(01:22:05)：我职业生涯初期做的工作，就其产生的影响而言，感觉并没有那么重要，但就我自己的判断力、自己的品味，以及我如何去做那些非常快速的研判而言，它确实感觉是脱胎换骨的。(01:22:27)：现在，如果我没有花多年去学习，我根本做不到这些。我以前做社交媒体，那种必须把我想要说的话压缩到 120 个字符、或者旧 Twitter 上是多少来着，240，我记不得了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I forget, actually, isn't that crazy? I forget what the original was. I think it was 140. Okay, 140 characters, yeah.
turns.zh: 我忘了，其实，是不是很疯狂？我忘了最初是多少了。我觉得是 140。对，140 个字符。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: 140, I think. It was short. And if you had to get a link in there, good luck to you. (01:22:55): But oh my gosh, my ability to just look at something written today, and just cut it, that text in half, third, whatever it needs to fill the space, I can do that in my sleep, because I got all these reps very early in my career. (01:23:10): I think people see the way that there's a threat of companies not wanting to hire as much entry-level talent, because it's like, "Oh, this is the kind of work that AI can do." (01:23:24): The fear that I hear, at least, is if you're not getting those reps early in your career, maybe it's not contributing so much value to the company at that moment, but it's how you learn to be great later on. (01:23:38): And so, there's a fear that in five, 10 years, we're just not going to have that class of people, who have learned to do the jobs well, and who have built judgment in that way. (01:23:48): But what I think that misses is, it assumes that you go and you do this analyst job for two years, and at the end of it you have a person who knows how to make models really well, knows how to do a few things really well. But why does that have to take two years? Why does that model of you grind over this thing? (01:24:12): You wait for feedback. Eventually, you get that feedback. Maybe that feedback's good, maybe it's not. You go back, you try again. It actually is really inefficient, when you think about it. (01:24:22): And the sort of learning applicAttions around AI that I get really excited about are, how do you shrink that loop? So in my podcast with Claire, I showed her how I build these GPTs, that kind of think like me. And the purpose of that is so that my team can get feedback that is at least 80% close to the feedback that I would be giving them. (01:24:44): But instead of having to wait until I get to their message, or until our one on one, they can get that on demand as many times as they want forever. And I think there's a lot of things like this, of ways that things that require other people, just naturally slow things down, require getting feedback from other people, just naturally slow things down. (01:25:06): We can build AI tools that, in my view, there's no reason why the amount of reps that you get at whatever task you're doing, you can be a film editor, just sitting there, poring over the film, deciding what to edit, what to cut, what to put into the trailer, or whatever it's making. That's an incredibly tedious job that takes forever. (01:25:29): And I think there's no reason we can't make that way more efficient with AI, that make the learning more fun. And so, I think that that's sort of my hot take is yes, there is this threat of, a lot of these jobs that are things that seem like you can just automate them away, that might happen. (01:25:52): But we absolutely still need to be investing in people's skills. I just don't think we need to be investing in them historically in the way that we always have. And I think in the future, we'll find that those ways actually seem quite inefficient, compared to what's possible today.
turns.zh: 140，我想。它很短。而且如果你还得在里面塞个链接，祝你好运。(01:22:55)：但是天哪，我现在只要看一眼今天写的东西，就能把它砍掉一半、三分之一，或者为了满足篇幅需要的任何比例，我闭着眼睛都能做，因为我在职业生涯的早期就获得了所有这些重复练习。(01:23:10)：我觉得人们看到了这样一种威胁——公司不想再招那么多初级人才，因为"哦，这是 AI 能做的那种工作。"(01:23:24)：至少我听到的恐惧是，如果你在职业生涯早期没有得到那些重复练习，也许那一刻它对公司贡献的价值没那么大，但那正是你学会日后变得出色的方式。(01:23:38)：所以，人们担心，五年、十年后，我们就不会有那样一类人——那些学会了把工作做好、并以那种方式建立起了判断力的人。(01:23:48)：但我觉得这忽略了的是，它假设你去做了两年分析师的工作，到头来你成了一个非常会建模型、非常会做几件事的人。但为什么一定要花两年？为什么一定要是那种你在这件事上死磕的模式？(01:24:12)：你等反馈。最终，你得到反馈。也许那反馈是好的，也许不是。你回去，再试一次。仔细想想，这其实效率很低。(01:24:22)：而让我真正兴奋的、围绕 AI 的学习应用，是：你如何缩短那个循环？所以在我和 Claire 的播客里，我向她展示了我如何构建这些"像我一样思考"的 GPT。其目的就是让我的团队能得到至少 80% 接近我会给他们的那种反馈。(01:24:44)：但不用等到我去到他们的消息、或等到我们的一对一，他们可以按需、想多少次就多少次、永远地获取反馈。而我觉得这里有个……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a powerful point. And we're already seeing this. I imagine you've seen these studies, I think it's in Nigeria, where they give students AI tutors, and they just zoom to the next, they accelerate so quickly in their progression of just reading and math. (01:26:21): I think we're already seeing it. And it's harder to measure in PM and product, and all these things, but in school, it's a lot easier to measure, and we're already seeing results there.
turns.zh: 这是非常有力的观点。而且我们已经在看到这一点了。我想你看过那些研究，我记得是在尼日利亚，他们给学生 AI 导师，然后学生就飞速进步，在读写和数学上的进展加速得非常快。(01:26:21)：我觉得我们已经在看到它了。在产品经理和产品这类领域更难衡量，但在学校里容易衡量得多，而且我们已经在那里看到结果了。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, 100%.
turns.zh: 对，完全同意。

turns.en: And to make this very real for people, you have this specific GPT, I think it's called Socrates, or what is called?

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Give an example, just to give people a sense of what this can do.

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, so this came from, I was talking earlier about learning how to make a really strong, logical argument, or just a strong argument for your point of view, in general. And the sort of fundamental skill for that, in my view, is logical thinking, logical reasoning. And when I think about the best way, we have to test that today, at least ...
turns.zh: 对，所以这源于，我之前聊到学习如何构建一个非常有说服力、符合逻辑的观点，或者总的来说，就是为你的立场构建一个有力的论证。而我认为，那项基础技能是逻辑思维、逻辑推理。而当我思考今天我们必须测试它的最好方式，至少……

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Think about the best way we have to test that today, at least the best is maybe not the right word, but the standard way we have to test that, the LSAT, the test that you take to get into law school, that is what that tests. And it sort of gives you these different scenarios and we'll try to say if a is true, then which of the following is true, is not true? Sort of testing some of these different logical relationships. (01:27:26): And so what I did was I made a GPT that I basically told it, "Create LSAT style questions to test logical reasoning, but put them in the scenarios of things that a PM would encounter." And I have a version of this that's very specific to WHOOP and working in consumer health, but you could do it for anything or you can just do generic, however you want to do it. (01:27:49): And actually it's kind of fun because it gives you the scenario and it's like, "The sales team is telling you that we need to invest in feature A and the, I don't know, the engineering team is telling you that we only have time to do feature B and the metrics are telling you that people who get this feature retain better." It just sort of gives you these little things and it's like, follow that logic, which is the logically best path from this? And it gives you a little multiple choice answer, you select one and it explains why you're right or wrong. (01:28:29): And so I think that's just another example of, you can't create those hyper personalized learnings, where I can make one that is literally so specific to you and your life, but is testing and training you on this broader skill set. And I think you can make things more fun that way, even in just the school context, in terms of doing that in a way that's just relevant to a person's interest, relevant to the things they care about. I think there's a ton of really interesting potential there too.
turns.zh: 想想我们今天测试它的最好方式，至少"最好"也许不是正确的词，但我们必须测试它的标准方式，就是 LSAT（法学院入学考试），也就是你想进法学院要考的那个试，它考的就是这个。它会给你这些不同的情境，然后试着让你判断：如果 A 为真，那么以下哪个为真、哪个不为真？就是测试这些不同的逻辑关系。(01:27:26)：所以我做了一个 GPT，我基本上是这么告诉它的："创建 LSAT 风格的题目来测试逻辑推理，但把它们放在产品经理会遇到的情境里。"而我有一个版本是特别针对 WHOOP、针对消费健康领域的，但你可以用在任何事情上，或者就做通用的，随你怎么弄。(01:27:49)：实际上这挺有趣的，因为它给你情境，比如"销售团队告诉你我们需要投资功能 A，而，我不知道，工程团队告诉你我们只有时间做功能 B，而指标告诉你拿到这个功能的人留存更好。"它就给你这些小东西，然后说，顺着那个逻辑，从这里面哪条是逻辑上最优的路径？它给你几个选择题答案，你选一个，它会解释你为什么对或错。(01:28:29)：所以我觉得这只是另一个例子——你无法创造出那种极度个性化的学习，而我可以做一个如此贴合你和你的生活的版本，同时又在测试和训练你那套更广泛的能力。而且我觉得你可以让事情变得更有趣，哪怕只是在学校情境下，用一种与个人兴趣、与他们在乎的事情相关的方式去做。我觉得那里也有大量非常有趣的潜力。

turns.zh: 我觉得这极其酷。我们会链接到它。大家一定要玩玩这个。好，我要带大家进入播客的两个固定环节（corners），然后在我们进入一个非常精彩的快问快答之前，我想聊聊 WHOOP。所以这是一个我在尝试的新环节，我打算叫它"关键转折点"（Pivotal Corner）。问题是：你职业生涯中最关键的转折点是什么？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: I mean I think it was at my former company, at Big Health, when my former boss left the company and I started reporting to the CEO. And again, I think it was my first time working with a CEO so closely, and it just, definitely trial by fire. But it made me understand so many things that seemed like they didn't make sense to me before, when I was just in the rank and file of a big tech company earlier in my career. You get in the room and you talk to these people and you're like, "Oh, this actually makes sense. I understand why this person has come to these conclusions." (01:31:36): And some of it's understanding the pressure they're under. Some of it's understanding, again, the way they view the world. But I think that was, to get to our earlier point around the humility of understanding that maybe this person is right about something that I don't see and maybe I can start by... If I start by giving them the benefit of the doubt, it is not only a nice thing to do, but it is also, it will help me understand why they're doing the things that they are. And I think I would've been so much less frustrated earlier in my career if I understood that instead of just being like, "Oh, this doesn't make any sense from where I'm sitting, so therefore it must not make any sense."
turns.zh: 我觉得是在我之前的公司 Big Health，当时我的前老板离开了公司，我开始向 CEO 汇报。再说一次，那是我第一次如此密切地和一位 CEO 共事，绝对是火线洗礼（trial by fire）。但它让我理解了很多之前在我职业生涯早期、还只是大科技公司里普通一员时，觉得说不通的事情。你进了那个房间，和这些人交谈，然后你会像"哦，这其实说得通。我理解这个人为什么会得出这些结论了。"(01:31:36)：其中一部分是理解他们承受的压力。一部分是去理解，再次，他们看待世界的方式。但我觉得，回到我们之前那个点——关于谦逊地理解，也许这个人在某件我看不到的事情上是对的，也许我可以从……如果我一开始就给他们以善意的假设，这不仅是一件好事，而且它也会帮我理解他们为什么在做他们所做的事。我觉得如果我早一点明白这一点，而不是只是想"哦，从我这个位置看这根本说不通，所以那一定就是说不通"，我在职业生涯早期的挫败感就会少得多。

turns.en: It's so cool that this connects back to your habit of doing this, having seen it, and being like, "Oh, I see, this is why..."
turns.zh: 这和你做这件事的习惯连起来了，真的很酷——你看到之后，就会像"哦，我明白了，这就是为什么……"

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, I guess I hadn't realized.
turns.zh: 是的，我想我之前没意识到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe I'm wrong, maybe I could be wrong.
turns.zh: 也许我错了，也许我可能错了。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Well, I mean that's what it is. I feel like I've had so many of those times where I don't know, when I was growing up, I felt so confident in how I felt about everything. And then you get out there and you're just like, "Oh, I was missing some things." And after a while you're kind of like, "Okay, maybe I should approach these situations a little differently with the possibility that maybe I'm missing something."

turns.en: So I actually asked your boss Kelvin, which is an awesome name by the way, Kelvin, about this moment. When I asked him what to ask you, and he brought this up actually, and here's the way, described it, "She may describe it as being thrown into the deep end or baptism by fire, but the reality is that she had the core skills and this was simply an opportunity for her to let those shine even more. turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Thanks Kelvin. That's really nice.
turns.zh: 谢谢 Kelvin。那真的很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He also said, "I wonder if she remembers how terrified she was now, because she absolutely knocked it out of the park and it felt like it was an inflection point that grew her confidence significantly."
turns.zh: 他还说："我想知道她现在还记不记得当时有多害怕，因为她绝对是打出了全垒打，感觉那是一个显著增长了她自信的转折点。"

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Oh, I was terrified. Yeah. Big time terrified. And then, I mean this is also what I was saying about why it's so important to be regimented about having these things outside of work that allow you to continue to thrive, even in the face of just utter feelings of failure, of, "I am not doing a good job, this is not going well. I don't know what I'm doing." A lot of it was that time. Kelvin actually gave me some great advice that, this is maybe kind of scary advice, but when I asked him what his advice for me with the time was, and he said, "Product leadership is the type of role where if you are not in control of the voices in your head, they will eat you alive." (01:34:16): And I think it's right. As I said, it is so often this feeling like there is not a clear right answer and not even necessarily a good answer. And everyone is looking to you for clarity and everyone is looking to you to make the right decisions and everyone sees the errors, or at least everyone can spot the flaws in whatever decision you make or whatever recommendation you make. And as I said, every path forward has flaws that can be poked in it. And so understanding that the existence of potential ways to be criticized about something does not warrant criticism in a way that can, I think often result in a lot of negative self-talk for people. So yeah, I mean it had a tremendous impact on me.
turns.zh: 哦，我当时害怕极了。对。非常害怕。而且，我的意思是，这也正是我为什么说，在业余时间保持那些能让你持续茁壮成长的事情、并对此保持自律是如此重要——哪怕面对的是彻底的失败感，那种"我做得不好，这进展不顺。我不知道我在干什么"的感觉。那段时间很大程度上就是这种状态。Kelvin 其实给了我一些很棒的建议，这也许是某种有点吓人的建议，但当我问他在那段时间给我的建议是什么时，他说："产品领导力这种角色，如果你不能控制自己脑海里的那些声音，它们会把你活活吃掉。"(01:34:16)：我觉得他说得对。如我所说，常常就是那种感觉：没有一个清晰的正确答案，甚至不一定有个好答案。每个人都在指望你给出清晰度，每个人都在指望你做出正确决定，而每个人都能看到错误——或者至少，无论你做出什么决定或提出什么建议，大家都能挑出其中的毛病。而如我所说，每条前进的道路都有可以被戳中的缺陷。所以要理解：某件事存在被批评的潜在可能，并不意味着就值得批评——而那种批评，我觉得常常会导致人们大量的负面自我对话。所以是的，我的意思是，这对我有巨大的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting you have so much of these habits and skills you've built seem to, it's clear where they come from, from all these experiences that you had.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你建立的这么多习惯和技能，似乎都清楚地源自你所有的这些经历。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Well, and to the point of when you start talking to people and you start trying to build this mental model of how they think, that's exactly what you learn, is well, I can see how this person worked at this company at this time and I can see how this person had this kind of relationship with this other person. And all of these things shape the way that we approach problems and the way that we try to just move through the world. And it is understanding those types of things that allow you to understand how a person thinks.
turns.zh: 嗯，而且说到你开始和人们交谈、开始试着建立他们如何思考的心理模型这一点，那正是你学到的——嗯，我能看到这个人在那个时间在这家公司工作过，我也能看到这个人和另一个人之间有那种关系。所有这些事情塑造了我们处理问题的方式，以及我们试图在这个世界上前行的方式。而正是理解那些类型的事情，让你能够理解一个人是如何思考的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder if you could ask ChatGPT to build, or Claude to build, these mental models. Like, "Here's their LinkedIn, here's their bio, here's a few things, how do they see the world?"
turns.zh: 我在想，你能不能让 ChatGPT 或 Claude 来构建这些心理模型。比如"这是他们的 LinkedIn，这是他们的简介，这是几件事，他们是怎么看世界的？"

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: I will admit that I have tried this. And I think it's a great idea. I think it does help. I have not gotten to a point where I'm comfortable sharing it with other people, nor have I told anyone that I have tried to do this for them, but I've certainly done it for myself. And I think it would be helpful. Because you could say things, you could upload a doc or whatever and be like, "What are the three questions that this person's going to ask me about it?" And then you could be prepared for the questions that person's going to ask you and that's great.
turns.zh: 我得承认我试过这个。而且我觉得这是个好主意。我觉得它确实有帮助。我还没到能舒服地把它分享给别人的程度，也没告诉过任何人我试着为他们做过这个，但我肯定为自己做过。而且我觉得那会很有帮助。因为你可以说，你可以上传一份文档之类的，然后说"这个人会就这件事问我哪三个问题？"然后你就能为那个人要问你的问题做好准备，那就很棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In this hypothetical example, what context do you share with this model to help it be good?
turns.zh: 在这个假设的例子里，你会和这个模型分享什么背景信息来让它表现得好？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Great question. Hypothetically, I told you that I take all these notes on, here's what this person said and here's how I interpret it, and LLMs are really good at pattern matching and sort of spotting the... You could feed all of those in and just say, "Come up with the 10 criteria that this person is most likely to use to assess a possible recommendation or path forward," or, "Give me the top 10 ways that this person is likely to pick apart an argument or object to something," and you're going to get a good answer.
turns.zh: 好问题。假设性地，我告诉过你，我会就这个人说过什么、我如何解读它，记下所有这些笔记，而 LLM 真的很擅长模式匹配和发现……你可以把所有这些都喂进去，然后就说"想出这个人最有可能用来评估一个可能建议或前进路径的 10 条标准"，或者"给我这个人最可能用来拆穿一个论点或反对某件事的 top 10 方式"，你会得到一个好答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: More reason to build this habit of taking notes and sharing with your team. On the other hand, this might also be a good use case for Granola or something like that where you have all these meeting notes and you could just feed it, "Here's all the things Hilary said," and, "Oh, what is she probably going to say about this?"
turns.zh: 这就更有理由去建立这个记笔记并与团队分享的习惯了。另一方面，这可能也是 Granola 或类似工具的一个好用例——你拥有所有这些会议笔记，你可以直接喂给它，"这是 Hilary 说过的所有事"，然后"哦，她大概会对这件事说什么？"

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, so cool. Okay, next corner, I'm going to take us to Fail Corner. So the question is, is there a story you could share of failure in your career where things didn't go the way you hoped and what you learned from that experience?
turns.zh: 哇，太酷了。好，下一个环节，我要带大家进入"失败角落"（Fail Corner）。在"失败角落"里，理念是：人们上这个播客，会分享所有这些胜利和成功，一切都在向右上角（上升）发展、精彩绝伦，但现实中事情并不总是那么顺利。所以问题是，你能分享一个你职业生涯中失败的故事吗——那些事没有按你希望的方式发展，以及你从那段经历中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: I mean I think the one that probably looms largest in my mind is, I mentioned this depression therapeutic that I spent about a year working on, and ultimately the company ended up acquiring a different depression therapeutic. And we kind of ended up merging the two of them. And a lot of the stuff that we had initially built that I had really loved about this product we were working on didn't really ever end up seeing the light of day beyond the kind of testing that we had done around it. And it was heartbreaking because I wish this product existed. I look at it and I'm like, "This was a great product and we put so much heart and soul into it." (01:38:28): And I think the lesson that I learned from that is, I think there's always a shot clock. When you're working, especially on a zero to one product, I think it can be very easy to feel like you have the luxury of time, of just like, we got to take the time to figure this out and get it right and that's what's most important. But the sort of build versus buy question is always live and it's always fair. And whether you want to admit it, if you're the one working on it, and you probably don't, I didn't want to admit this, there is a point at which it makes more sense for the company. If it is taking too long to develop something and there is a solution out there that works, it is the right decision to acquire that. (01:39:15): I mean I worked at Dropbox where I saw this happen all the time where we would acquire products that other teams internally had been working on and it's just like, it's heartbreaking when it happens. But I think there's an urgency that that has instilled in me that I think is actually really good and healthy, especially again working in this era where there is kind of this AI arms race and everyone's trying to move really quickly of, yeah, there's always a shot clock. And you might not be aware of it, but it's there, and you got to build your heart out and you got to ship and you got to get things out because at any time, that clock might run out.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得在我脑海里最挥之不去的，可能是我之前提到过的那个抑郁症疗法产品，我花了大概一年时间在做它，而最终公司收购了另一种抑郁症疗法。我们某种意义上把两者合并了。而我们最初构建的、我真正热爱于这个产品的很多东西，除了我们围绕它做过的那种测试之外，再也没真正见过天日。这让人心碎，因为我希望这个产品存在。我看着它就想"这是个很棒的产品，我们投入了那么多心血。"(01:38:28)：而我觉得我从中学到的教训是，我觉得永远都有一个"进攻时限"（shot clock）。当你在工作时，尤其是在做从零到一的产品时，我觉得很容易产生一种错觉，觉得自己有的是时间，就像"我们得花时间去搞清楚、做对，那才是最重要的事"。但"自建还是购买"这个问题始终是活着的、始终合理的。无论你是否愿意承认——如果你就是做这件事的人，你可能不愿意承认，我当时也不想承认——总有一个时点，对公司来说，收购反而是更合理的选择。如果开发某样东西花的时间太长，而市面上有可行的解决方案，那么收购它就是正确的决定。(01:39:15)：我是说，我在 Dropbox 工作时，看到这种事一直发生——我们会收购公司内部其他团队一直在做的产品，而发生时真的让人心碎。但我觉得这件事在我心里注入了一种紧迫感，我认为那其实非常好、非常健康，尤其是再次置身于这个 AI 军备竞赛、人人都想快速推进的时代——对，永远都有一个进攻时限。你可能没意识到它，但它就在那儿，你得全力以赴地去构建，你得发布，你得……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Yeah, I'm really excited you got it. I know you tried it before and...
turns.zh: 是的，你买了我真兴奋。我知道你之前试过，而且……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: People who have tried WHOOP in the past maybe felt like it was very focused on elite athletes and that is...
turns.zh: 过去试过 WHOOP 的人，也许觉得它非常聚焦于精英运动员，而那是……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's exactly what I felt.
turns.zh: 是的，那正是我的感觉。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Sort of the lifeblood of the company. And I think what we've done with our new experience is we've really built something that can help everyone be healthier and live better. I would say we're no longer just for elite athletes. We're really now a health and performance companion for anybody who wants to feel their best. (01:40:41): For the first time in our company's history, we've updated our mission, so we're now saying that WHOOP exists to unlock human performance and health span. And health span I think is, and I mentioned earlier this feature I'm really excited about, because I do think it is kind of the most powerful version of a longevity-type feature I have seen because it is so focused on your behaviors and your habits today. (01:41:06): And we built it to be super, super actionable. So rather than just giving you a score that you're kind of like, "Okay, that's nice," if you start sleeping even 20 minutes more, 30 minutes more tonight, you're going to see how that changes your case of aging. You're going to see how that changes your WHOOP age. And I think that, as I mentioned earlier, I think is really rewarding. (01:41:25): We also have a lot of personalized coaching through our AI in terms of actions that you can take to improve your WHOOP age, to improve your sleep, to feel better, and it's all part of our broader aim to make health more actionable and accessible. I think one thing I'm really excited about is we have a bunch of new women's health features, so we have hormonal insights with improved menstrual cycle tracking. I'm actually pregnant and I-
turns.zh: 可以说是公司的命脉。而我觉得我们通过新体验所做的事情，是真正打造了能帮助每个人更健康、生活得更好的东西。我会说，我们不再只服务于精英运动员。我们现在真的是任何想要感觉最佳状态之人的健康与表现伴侣。(01:40:41)：在公司历史上，我们第一次更新了使命，所以现在我们说，WHOOP 的存在是为了释放人类的表现与健康寿命（health span）。而健康寿命，我觉得——我之前提到过这个让我非常兴奋的功能——因为我认为它是我见过的那种"长寿类"功能中力量最强的一个版本，因为它如此聚焦于你今天的行为和习惯。(01:41:06)：而且我们把它做得超级、超级可操作。所以与其只是给你一个分数、让你像"好吧，还不错"那样，如果你今晚多睡哪怕 20 分钟、30 分钟，你就会看到那如何改变了你的衰老情况。你会看到那如何改变了你的 WHOOP 年龄。而我觉得，如我之前所说，这真的很有奖励感。(01:41:25)：我们还通过 AI 提供了大量个性化指导，关于你可以采取哪些行动来改善你的 WHOOP 年龄、改善睡眠、感觉更好，而这一切都是我们更宏大目标的一部分——让健康变得更具可操作性和可及性。我觉得有一件我非常兴奋的事是我们有一堆新的女性健康功能，所以我们有结合改善后月经周期追踪的荷尔蒙洞察。我其实怀孕了，而且我——

turns.en: What? I didn't know that. That's a big announcement. Wow. Congratulations Hilary. That's so exciting.
turns.zh: 什么？我不知道这件事。那是个大公告啊。哇。恭喜你 Hilary。这太令人兴奋了。

turns.en: But actually part of how I found out I was pregnant was in seeing my WHOOP data.
turns.zh: 但其实我发现自己怀孕，有一部分是通过看我的 WHOOP 数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What? What? That's insane.
turns.zh: 什么？什么？那太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: In my WHOOP data, which is pretty remarkable.
turns.zh: 在我的 WHOOP 数据里，这相当了不起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: And the way that we have this cycle tracking now, you can see the way that your different, your HRV, your resting heart rate, things like that, that's your heart rate variability and your resting heart rate, fluctuates throughout different times of your cycle. And even in the time leading up to that, I had a not straightforward pregnancy journey, and having these tools to really understand what was going on in my body was tremendously helpful and tremendously empowering for me and honestly really has changed my life. So I'm really excited about that. (01:42:40): We have a lot of great new heart health features. We have a heart health screener with blood pressure insights and ECG. That's really cool. We got a lot of great stuff cooking. So even if you tried WHOOP in the past and thought it wasn't for you, I think the new experience is a real upgrade and it's something that I'm deeply proud of having worked on and really excited to have out in the world.
turns.zh: 而且我们现在这种周期追踪的方式，你可以看到你的不同指标——你的 HRV（心率变异性）、你的静息心率，诸如此类的——也就是你的心率变异性和你的静息心率——在你周期的不同阶段是如何波动的。甚至在那之前的那段时间，我的怀孕之路并不顺利，而拥有这些工具去真正理解我身体里在发生什么，对我来说是极大的帮助、极大的赋能，老实说真的改变了我的生活。所以我对那感到非常兴奋。(01:42:40)：我们还有很多很棒的新心脏健康功能。我们有一个带血压洞察和心电图（ECG）的心脏健康筛查器。那真的很酷。我们还有一大堆很棒的东西在开发中。所以即使你过去试过 WHOOP、觉得它不适合你，我觉得新体验是一次真正的升级，而且这是我深感自豪参与打造、并真正兴奋能推向世界的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am genuinely very excited about this. You could do, you said blood pressure and VO2 max?
turns.zh: 我对此真的非常兴奋。你说可以测血压和 VO2 Max？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.en: And I know the battery is even longer too. There's just so much stuff.
turns.zh: 而且我知道电池续航也更长了。东西实在是太多了。

turns.en: Oh, we have a 14 day battery life. I didn't even say. We have these beautiful new leather bands which I love.
turns.zh: 哦，我们有 14 天的电池续航。我还没说到这个。我们还有这些漂亮的新皮革表带，我很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哦哇。

turns.en: Okay. 14 day battery's life is insane. I'm going on vacation tomorrow and I don't even need to bring a charger. This is fantastic.
turns.zh: 好。14 天的电池续航简直疯狂。我明天就去度假了，我甚至都不需要带充电器。这太棒了。

turns.en: Oh man. This sounds like a WHOOP ad, but I'm very excited about this.
turns.zh: 哦天哪。这听起来像是个 WHOOP 广告，但我对此非常兴奋。

So really excited about that too.
turns.zh: 我再说一件事，就是我们为 Advanced Labs（高级实验室）开了一个等候名单，所以很快你就能在应用里做全面的实验室检测了，而且我觉得我们聊到健康的未来，就是能在一个地方掌控你所有的健康数据，然后不仅能从中找到信号、理解你的睡眠如何影响你的代谢健康之类的事情。而且再次，能得到真正可操作的指导，关于你可以采取哪些行动来感觉更好、达到最健康的状态，并且只是不断推进我们拉进 WHOOP 生态系统中的所有数据的边界。所以我也对此非常兴奋。

turns.en: I'm hoping the WHOOP can actually take my blood and labs. Is that where this is going? Because that'd be so convenient.
turns.zh: 我希望 WHOOP 真的能抽我的血、做实验室检测。这是要往那个方向走吗？因为那会太方便了。

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: No comment.
turns.zh: 不予置评。

turns.en: Okay. It'd be weird but also awesome. I don't have to go anywhere to do that. Hilary, we covered so much ground. Before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you wanted to touch on? Anything else that we haven't covered that you think, or last nugget you wanted to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 好。那会有点怪，但也很棒。我都不用跑任何地方去做。Hilary，我们聊了这么多内容。在我们进入一个非常精彩的快问快答之前，还有什么你想提一下的吗？还有什么我们没覆盖到、你觉得值得一提的，或者是你想留给听众的最后一点心得？

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: I don't think so. I feel like we covered everything
turns.zh: 我觉得没有了。我感觉我们把一切都覆盖到了。

turns.en: We did. We covered so much. In the best way possible. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 是的。我们聊了这么多。以最好的方式。说到这，我们到了非常精彩的快问快答环节。你准备好了吗？

turns.en: I'm ready.

turns.zh: 你会最频繁地向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.en: Buddy, you can't call something a lightning round and then ask me about books. We could go for a whole other podcast where I'm like...

Even the business books I love the most that shaped how I think I'm like, "I kind of got the gist of them part way through," but fiction, I'm like, everybody should read East of Eden by John Steinbeck and everybody should read The Sun Also Rises by Ernest Hemingway, which is my comfort book. (01:45:22): I think what I love about fiction is it teaches you how to sit inside tension. I think so much of working in product is, as I said, you're in this fog and you just have to provide clarity and you have to be really good at providing structure to ambiguous things and finding the way forward and to succeed at the job, you have to be able to do that. But I also think to succeed as a human in the job, you have to be able to sit in the mess and sit in the ambiguity. John Keats, the poet, talks about this concept of negative capability, which is the ability to remain in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. And I love that.
turns.zh: 好，听着我要说的话，我要在这一点上彻底走小说路线。我会说，如果你要读一本书，别费劲去读商业书了。哪怕是我最爱、塑造了我思维方式的那些商业书，我也觉得"读到一半我就差不多 get 到要点了"，但小说，我就觉得，每个人都该读 John Steinbeck 的《伊甸之东》（East of Eden），每个人都该读 Ernest Hemingway 的《太阳照常升起》（The Sun Also Rises），那本是我的慰藉之书。(01:45:22)：我觉得我喜欢小说的地方在于，它教你如何安坐于张力之中。我觉得做产品工作很大一部分就是，如我所说，你身处迷雾，而你只能提供清晰度，你必须非常擅长为模糊的事情提供结构、找到前进的方向，而要在这份工作上成功，你必须能做到这一点。但我也觉得，要作为一个人在这个工作上成功，你必须能够安坐于混乱、安坐于模糊。诗人 John Keats 谈过"negative capability"（消极能力）这个概念，就是能够停留在不确定、神秘、怀疑之中，而不急躁地去抓事实和理由。我很喜欢这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny

In the, "I'm going to break down this problem, I'm going to structure it, I'm going to get out, but also I'm going to sit here and I'm going to accept that there is no right answer and there is no perfect answer." And that's life. You don't learn that from... To the extent that you learn that from a book at all, which maybe you don't, but I think you can learn it in fiction.
turns.zh: 没错。而且你得两者兼具，对吧。再说一次，小说，我喜欢二元对立。小说里有很多二元对立，很多人内心有相互冲突的力量，既能如此驱动人，也能成为那么多痛苦的源头。我觉得活在两者之中很重要。也就是"我要拆解这个问问题、我要结构化它、我要搞出来，但同时我也要坐在这里，接受根本没有正确答案、也没有完美答案。"那就是人生。你没法从……在你能从书里学到那点的程度内——也许你根本学不到——但我觉得你能从小说里学到它。

We want it all to be the cool parts, but it can't. So thank you Beavis and Butthead.

turns.speaker: Hilary Gridley
turns.en: There's a poem by Derek Walcott about, it's called Sea Grapes, and it's about Odysseus, and he talks about Odysseus being driven by the ancient war between obsession and responsibility. And I read that line when I was 18 years old and it has always stuck with me. And I sort of mentioned earlier, I think about these dualities that drive us. And I think as a product person, I always feel like I'm living between these two, the obsession and the responsibility. I want to go so deep on this and I want to spend as much time as I possibly can just sorting every little piece out. (01:51:48): But we live in a society, we exist in a business. I am trying to create value for shareholders and trying to bring these two things together, I feel like a, has been the kind of defining struggle of my career, I think of many people's careers, is how you have something that you feel like you can really obsess over and have that flow over, or have that flow when you're working on. But then it's got to kind of work in this broader system as well. And I think that's sort of been the thing that I think of as the guiding post for what I want to do with my career and with my life. So I think it's got to be Derek Walcott.
